title: Array Tasks and Access Patterns
summary: Section divider introducing strategies and questions to determine coding approaches for array tasks and access patterns.
main_text: Strategies and questions to ask to determine coding approaches. Array Tasks and Access Patterns.
notes_text: Section header slide transitioning into the main content of the unit.

title: Sequential vs. Random Access
summary: Distinguishes between sequential access (iterating through all elements with a loop) and random access (computing a single index to access one element directly).
main_text: Most array-based tasks fall into either a sequential-access pattern or random-access pattern. Sequential access iterates (loops) through all elements. Used for tasks that require looking at all elements in the worst case. Random access computes the ONE index to access. Used for tasks that only require accessing one specific element. Sequential access example: int total = 0; for(int i=0; i < 20; i++){ total += scores[i]; } This loops through a scores array of 20 elements summing them. Random access example: int stuID; cout << "Enter ID\n"; cin >> stuID; cout << "Your score: "; cout << scores[stuID]; cout << endl; This uses the student ID directly as the index to look up one score.
notes_text: Key conceptual distinction for the unit. Sequential access uses a loop; random access computes the index directly from input.

images.description: Two side-by-side diagrams of a scores array (indices 0-19, addresses 520-1076). Left shows sequential access with a pink arrow sweeping across all elements and a for-loop summing them. Right shows random access where a stuID variable (value 2) points directly to index 2 (value 93) with code that reads and outputs that single score.

title: Sequential Access
summary: Details the two main categories of sequential access tasks: combining all elements (sum, average, count-if, modify-all) and searching/selecting an element with potential early stopping.
main_text: To repeat: Use sequential access when you MUST (or POTENTIALLY need to) visit EVERY element. Common tasks that require sequential access: Combining ALL elements: Sum or average; Count-if (e.g. count how many 100s); Modify-all (e.g. increment all). Search / select an element potentially stopping (break) early (in an unsorted array): Find a particular value; Minimum / maximum.
notes_text: Two sub-categories: tasks that always visit every element (combine-all) vs. tasks that may stop early (search/select). Both use sequential access because in the worst case you may need to examine all elements.

images.description: Two array diagrams illustrating sequential access. Top: a scores array with a pink arrow sweeping across all elements and a 'sum' accumulator box, representing combine-all tasks. Bottom: a find(96) operation with a pink arrow scanning the array to locate value 96, representing search tasks.

title: Random Access Example: Player Scores
summary: Introduces a problem where 8 players compete by scoring points, and the task is to track scores using an array and determine the highest-scoring player.
main_text: Consider the problem of a game where 8 players compete by scoring points. Some players may score points faster than others. Track the score of the 8 players by reading in the ID of each player that scores a point. In the example input shown below: Player 4 scored, then player 3, then player 7, then player 6, etc. Player 4 scored the most with 3 points. Players scoring points (and their order): 4 3 7 6 4 6 5 4 1 2 -1. Highest Scoring Player: 4.
notes_text: This example motivates the use of random access to increment a player's score using the player ID as the array index. The -1 serves as a sentinel value to end input.

images.description: Input sequence '4 3 7 6 4 6 5 4 1 2 -1' shown in a box, with the result 'Highest Scoring Player: 4' displayed to the right.

title: Scratch Work
summary: Prompts students to think about what data to track and how to decompose the player scores problem into subtasks or phases.
main_text: What data do you need to track to answer this problem? Can you decompose this problem into multiple subtasks or 'phases'? Players scoring points (and their order): 4 3 7 6 4 6 5 4 1 2 -1. Highest Scoring Player: 4.
notes_text: Encourages problem decomposition before coding. Students should identify they need an array of scores and a way to find the maximum after tallying.

title: Player Score [1]
summary: Traces the first two steps of the player scores algorithm, showing how reading player IDs 4 and 3 from input uses random access to increment the corresponding indices in the points array.
main_text: Track the score of the 8 players by reading in the ID of each player that scores a point. As we read in the players who scored points, update the point array. Do we know what index to update? Or do we have to walk through the full array? Input: 4 3 7 6 4 6 5 4 1 2 -1. Left side: Reading player 4 (first input). Player (integer 0-7) = 4. The points array at index [4] is incremented from 0 to 1. Right side: Reading player 3 (second input). Player (integer 0-7) = 3. The points array at index [3] is incremented from 0 to 1. This is random access because we know exactly which index to update.
notes_text: The player ID directly maps to an array index, making this a random access pattern. No loop through the array is needed to update a score.

images.description: Two side-by-side diagrams showing the points array (8 elements, indices 0-7, addresses 520-548). Left: player ID 4 is read from input and an arrow points to index [4], showing value changing from 0 to 1. Right: player ID 3 is read and an arrow points to index [3], showing value changing from 0 to 1.

title: Player Score [2]
summary: Continues the trace with the third and fourth inputs (players 7 and 6), incrementing indices 7 and 6 in the points array.
main_text: Track the score of the 8 players by reading in the ID of each player that scores a point. As we read in the players who scored points, update the point array. Do we know what index to update? Or do we have to walk through the full array? Input: 4 3 7 6 4 6 5 4 1 2 -1. Left side: Reading player 7 (third input). The points array at index [7] is incremented from 0 to 1. Right side: Reading player 6 (fourth input). The points array at index [6] is incremented from 0 to 1.
notes_text: Continuation of the step-by-step trace. Each input is directly used as the index for the array update.

images.description: Two side-by-side diagrams of the points array. Left: player 7 is being processed, index [7] changes from 0 to 1. Right: player 6 is processed, index [6] changes from 0 to 1. Array state shows indices [3] and [4] already at 1 from previous steps.

title: Player Score [3]
summary: Continues the trace with the fifth and sixth inputs (player 4 again and player 6 again), showing how repeated player IDs increment existing values.
main_text: Track the score of the 8 players by reading in the ID of each player that scores a point. As we read in the players who scored points, update the point array. Do we know what index to update? Or do we have to walk through the full array? Input: 4 3 7 6 4 6 5 4 1 2 -1. Left side: Reading player 4 again (fifth input). The points array at index [4] is incremented from 1 to 2. Right side: Reading player 6 again (sixth input). The points array at index [6] is incremented from 1 to 2.
notes_text: Key observation: when a player scores again, their count increments beyond 1. Player 4 now has 2 points and player 6 now has 2 points.

images.description: Two side-by-side diagrams of the points array. Left: player 4 is read again, index [4] changes from 1 to 2. Right: player 6 is read again, index [6] changes from 1 to 2.

title: Player Score [3] (continued)
summary: Continues tracing inputs 5 and 4 (players 5 and 4 for the third time), showing player 4 reaching 3 points.
main_text: Track the score of the 8 players by reading in the ID of each player that scores a point. As we read in the players who scored points, update the point array. Do we know what index to update? Or do we have to walk through the full array? Input: 4 3 7 6 4 6 5 4 1 2 -1. Left side: Reading player 5 (seventh input). The points array at index [5] is incremented from 0 to 1 (not shown changing but implied from prior state). Right side: Reading player 4 for the third time (eighth input). The points array at index [4] would increment to 3 (not fully shown).
notes_text: Note: slides 9 and 10 both carry the title 'Player Score [3]' in the original deck. This appears to be a continuation covering inputs 7 and 8 in the sequence.

title: Player Score [4]
summary: Shows the final input steps (player 2 and sentinel -1) and the completed points array state after all inputs are processed.
main_text: What do we do when we run out of input? Input: 4 3 7 6 4 6 5 4 1 2 -1. Left side: Reading player 2 (ninth input). The points array at index [2] is incremented from 0 to 1. Right side: Reading -1 (sentinel value, tenth input). The -1 signals end of input and the loop stops. Final array state - points: [0] = 0, [1] = 1, [2] = 1, [3] = 1, [4] = 3, [5] = 1, [6] = 2, [7] = 1.
notes_text: The sentinel value -1 terminates the input loop. After processing, the complete points array is shown. Player 4 has the highest score of 3.

images.description: Three array diagrams. Top-left: processing player 2, index [2] changes from 0 to 1. Top-right: processing -1 (sentinel), loop stops. Bottom: final completed points array showing values [0,1,1,1,3,1,2,1] across indices 0-7.

title: Player Score [5]
summary: After tallying all scores via random access, uses sequential access to find the maximum value in the points array and determine the highest-scoring player.
main_text: What do we do when we run out of input? To produce the desired output, what do we have to track now? The maximum points? After the random-access phase completes and all scores are tallied, a sequential access (loop) through the points array is needed to find the maximum value. The points array contains: [0]=0, [1]=1, [2]=1, [3]=1, [4]=3, [5]=1, [6]=2, [7]=1. A pink arrow sweeps across all elements comparing each to a 'max' accumulator. The highest scoring player is 4 (with 3 points).
notes_text: This slide illustrates the two-phase approach: Phase 1 uses random access to tally scores, Phase 2 uses sequential access to find the max. This is a common pattern combining both access types.

images.description: The completed points array with a pink arrow sweeping across all elements to a 'max' accumulator box, illustrating the sequential search for the maximum. Lines connect each element to the max box. Result shows Highest Scoring Player = 4.
